question: Describe a situation where you had a conflict with a manager, peer, or someone senior to you. How did you handle it?

raiseTranscript.text: My manager and I disagreed on the priority of a bug fix versus a new feature. I gathered the data on customer impact and scheduled a short sync to walk through the numbers.
We agreed to split the sprint and fix the top two issues first. I learned to bring data earlier next time.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a situation where you had a conflict with a manager, peer, or someone senior to you. How did you handle it?
Role: new engineer on payments team; Situation: manager pushed feature over P1 bug
Actions: pulled usage data, proposed split, asked for feedback on approach
Outcome: sprint adjusted, bug fixed same week
Quote: "I learned to bring data earlier next time."
Follow-up: How did you feel bringing it up? Candidate: nervous but focused on the customer numbers.
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate owned their piece of the disagreement by preparing data and seeking a practical compromise rather than escalating or staying silent. The story shows they treated the manager as a partner and closed with a clear lesson about timing. This matches the level expectation of individual ownership and coachability. Biggest strength is the willingness to revisit their own approach after the fact.

lowerTranscript.text: My manager wanted to ship something I thought was broken so I just did what they said and fixed it later on my own.
Did you talk to them about your concern?
Not really, I didn't want to argue.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Role: junior dev; Situation: disagreed on shipping criteria
Actions: stayed quiet and worked around it afterward
Outcome: shipped with known issues, fixed in next cycle
Quote: "I didn't want to argue."
Follow-up: What would you do differently? Candidate: probably the same.
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The candidate avoided the conversation entirely and chose silent workarounds instead of raising the issue directly. No evidence of attempting to influence the outcome or learning from the situation. This signals low ownership of interpersonal resolution at even the individual-contributor level.

raiseTranscript.text: A peer on the platform team blocked my service migration over a shared dependency concern. I set up a working session with both teams and mapped the actual risk surface.
How did you get them to engage?
I asked what data would change their mind and we ran a small canary together. Migration went ahead with two extra guardrails.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Role: senior SDE; Situation: cross-team dependency conflict on migration timeline
Actions: initiated joint session, defined success criteria together, ran canary
Outcome: migration completed, added two permanent checks to the platform
Quote: "I asked what data would change their mind."
Follow-up: What if they still refused? Candidate: would have escalated with the joint findings.
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate used influence without authority by turning a blocking disagreement into a shared experiment and delivered a durable fix that benefited the platform. Story shows cross-team scope and a repeatable method rather than one-off persuasion. Biggest strength is converting conflict into a lasting improvement.

lowerTranscript.text: I escalated to my manager after the peer kept pushing back and let them sort it out.
I sent a couple of emails explaining my position.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Role: senior SDE; Situation: peer blocked migration
Actions: sent emails then escalated
Outcome: manager intervened, migration delayed two weeks
Quote: "I let them sort it out."
Follow-up: Did the relationship recover? Candidate: not really, we avoid each other now.
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The candidate defaulted to escalation after minimal direct effort and left the relationship damaged. No attempt to find shared data or create a joint path forward. This falls short of the cross-team influence expected at senior level.

raiseTranscript.text: Two of my engineers were in open conflict over code ownership on a critical service. I brought them together with clear expectations and had each present their view plus proposed guardrails.
We landed on a shared on-call rotation and a review checklist. Both engineers later said the structure reduced friction and one was promoted the next cycle.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Role: engineering manager; Situation: direct-report conflict on ownership
Actions: structured discussion, defined decision rights, followed up on outcomes
Outcome: process created, one promotion, lower escalation rate
Quote: "Both engineers later said the structure reduced friction."
Follow-up: How did you handle the stronger personality? Candidate: gave equal airtime and documented agreements.
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The candidate treated the conflict as a team process problem, created durable mechanisms, and tied the outcome to development of the people involved. Evidence of owning team dynamics rather than just mediating one incident. Biggest strength is the follow-through that produced a promotion and reduced future friction.

lowerTranscript.text: I told them to work it out and come back when they had a plan.
Not really, they stopped bringing it up so I assumed it was fine.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Role: EM; Situation: two reports in conflict
Actions: delegated resolution without structure or follow-up
Outcome: issue went underground, one engineer transferred teams
Quote: "I assumed it was fine."
Follow-up: What signals did you miss? Candidate: none until the transfer request.
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The candidate delegated the conflict without providing process or accountability and missed the downstream impact. No evidence of developing the team or owning the outcome. This is below the level of handling underperformance and team dynamics expected from a manager.

raiseTranscript.text: Our sales and engineering orgs were misaligned on roadmap priorities, creating repeated escalations to the CEO. I ran a joint offsite to surface the underlying incentive mismatch and redefined the planning cadence with shared OKRs.
What changed at the org level?
Escalations dropped 70 percent and we hit the next two quarters' revenue targets without emergency reprioritization.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Role: VP Engineering; Situation: org-level conflict between sales and eng on priorities
Actions: diagnosed incentive mismatch, redesigned planning process, introduced shared OKRs
Outcome: 70 percent fewer escalations, revenue targets met
Quote: "Escalations dropped 70 percent."
Follow-up: How did you handle the sales leader who resisted? Candidate: used their own pipeline data to show the cost of churn.
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The candidate identified a systemic conflict between two organizations, changed the operating rhythm, and delivered measurable business impact. Story demonstrates strategic judgment and long-term leverage rather than case-by-case mediation. Biggest strength is tying resolution directly to revenue outcomes.

lowerTranscript.text: I met with the sales VP a few times and we agreed to communicate better.
Somewhat, but we still had to escalate the big roadmap fights.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Role: VP Eng; Situation: sales-eng priority conflict
Actions: bilateral meetings and verbal agreement to communicate
Outcome: continued escalations on major decisions
Quote: "We still had to escalate the big roadmap fights."
Follow-up: What structural change did you consider? Candidate: none, focused on relationship.
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. The candidate treated an org-level misalignment as a relationship issue and produced no durable process change. Continued escalations show lack of strategic leverage. This falls short of the business-impact and long-term thinking required at the executive level.

diagnostic.junior: Raises when candidate initiates conversation with data
diagnostic.senior: Raises when candidate creates joint experiment across teams
diagnostic.manager: Raises when candidate imposes structure and follows up
diagnostic.exec: Raises when candidate redesigns operating rhythm between orgs
Org-level planning change tied to business metrics

diagnostic.senior: Leaves working relationship intact or improved
diagnostic.manager: Both parties able to continue productively
diagnostic.exec: Organizations continue to collaborate without ongoing mediation
